content: The network layout visualisations in Figure 2 B–E give an intuitive picture of the effect of the sparsification. The highly sparse graphs obtained when the number of neighbours $k$ is very small are not robust. As $k$ is increased, the local similarities between documents induce the formation of dense subgraphs (which appear closer in the graph visualisation layout). When the number of neighbours becomes too large, the local structure becomes diffuse and the subgraphs lose coherence, signalling the degradation of the local graph structure. Figure 2 shows that the MST-kNN graph with $k=13$ presents a reasonable balance between local and global structure. Relatively sparse graphs that preserve important edges and global connectivity of the dataset (guaranteed here by the MST) have computational advantages when using community detection algorithms.
